claim: Pom1 kinase forms gradients with maxima at cell poles in Schizosaccharomyces pombe rod-shaped cells.
source: In Schizosaccharomyces pombe rod-shaped cells, Pom1 kinase forms gradients with maxima at cell poles.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of Pom1.

claim: Pom1 controls the timing of mitotic entry by inhibiting Cdr2.
source: Pom1 controls the timing of mitotic entry by inhibiting Cdr2, which forms stable membrane-associated nodes at mid-cell.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pom1 gradients rely on membrane association regulated by a phosphorylation-dephosphorylation cycle.
source: Pom1 gradients rely on membrane association regulated by a phosphorylation-dephosphorylation cycle and lateral diffusion modulated by clustering.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Individual Pom1 molecules bind the membrane too transiently to diffuse from pole to mid-cell.
source: Using quantitative PALM imaging, we find individual Pom1 molecules bind the membrane too transiently to diffuse from pole to mid-cell.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by PALM imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Pom1 molecules exchange within longer lived clusters forming the functional gradient unit.
source: Instead, we propose they exchange within longer lived clusters forming the functional gradient unit.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on PALM imaging and TIRF data showing cluster dynamics.

claim: Multi-phosphorylation shapes and buffers the Pom1 gradient to control mid-cell levels.
source: An allelic series blocking auto-phosphorylation shows that multi-phosphorylation shapes and buffers the gradient to control mid-cell levels, which represent the critical Cdr2-regulating pool.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from the phospho-site mutant allelic series in Figure 4.

claim: More Pom1 overlaps with Cdr2 in short than long cells.
source: TIRF imaging of this cortical pool demonstrates more Pom1 overlaps with Cdr2 in short than long cells, consistent with Pom1 inhibition of Cdr2 decreasing with cell growth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by TIRF imaging data in Figure 6.

claim: Pom1 gradients modulate Pom1 mid-cell levels according to cell size.
source: Thus, the gradients modulate Pom1 mid-cell levels according to cell size.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by TIRF imaging data.

claim: Pom1 is nucleated at cell poles upon dephosphorylation by a type I phosphatase complex whose regulatory subunit Tea4 is delivered by microtubules.
source: Pom1 gradients are nucleated at cell poles upon dephosphorylation by a type I phosphatase complex whose regulatory subunit Tea4 is delivered by microtubules (Hachet et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2005; Tatebe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Pom1 reveals a lipid-binding activity that maps to a 200-aa region in its N-terminal half.
source: Dephosphorylation of Pom1 reveals a lipid-binding activity that maps to a 200-aa region in its N-terminal half.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: At the plasma membrane, Pom1 forms small clusters and is thought to laterally diffuse.
source: At the plasma membrane, Pom1 forms small clusters and is thought to laterally diffuse (Hachet et al., 2011; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pom1 undergoes autophosphorylation reactions that promote its detachment from the membrane, leading to the graded pattern.
source: It also undergoes autophosphorylation reactions that promote its detachment from the membrane, leading to the graded pattern (Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Pom1 gradients exhibit a noise correction mechanism that compensates for large variations in protein concentration at the cell poles.
source: An interesting feature of Pom1 gradients is a noise correction mechanism that compensates for large variations in protein concentration at the cell poles, which can vary up to fourfold (Hersch et al., 2015; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In the Pom1 gradient, the decay length is independent of the amplitude at the pole in a simple diffusive gradient.
source: In a simple diffusive gradient, the decay length (the distance at which the concentration is reduced to a certain fraction of its amplitude) is independent of the amplitude at the pole.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical comparison in the introduction.

claim: The Pom1 gradient is corrected by varying the slope of the gradient decay: gradients with higher Pom1 concentration have a steeper decay, while those with lower Pom1 concentration have a flatter decay.
source: In contrast, the Pom1 gradient is corrected by varying the slope of the gradient decay: gradients with higher Pom1 concentration have a steeper decay, while those with lower Pom1 concentration have a flatter decay.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known property of Pom1 gradients.

claim: One model suggests gradient buffering is the consequence of concentration-dependent inter-molecular phosphorylation, which promotes Pom1 detachment from the membrane.
source: One model suggests gradient buffering is the consequence of concentration-dependent inter-molecular phosphorylation, which promotes Pom1 detachment from the membrane (Hersch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a proposed model with a supporting citation.

claim: A second model hypothesizes that buffering results from concentration-dependent clustering of Pom1, with higher concentrations leading to larger, slower diffusive clusters, causing a traffic-jam effect at the cell tips.
source: A second model hypothesizes that buffering results from concentration-dependent clustering of Pom1, with higher concentrations leading to larger, slower diffusive clusters, causing a traffic-jam effect at the cell tips (Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an alternative proposed model with a supporting citation.

claim: pom1∆ cells divide off-center.
source: First, Pom1 provides spatial information for division site positioning: pom1∆ cells divide off-center (Bähler and Nurse, 2001; Bähler and Pringle, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: pom1∆ cells divide precociously at an aberrantly small size.
source: Second, Pom1 provides temporal information to regulate the timing of mitotic entry: pom1∆ cells divide precociously at an aberrantly small size (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pom1 directly phosphorylates the SAD-family kinase Cdr2 on different residues for its two functions.
source: For both functions, Pom1 directly phosphorylates the SAD-family kinase Cdr2, but on different residues (Bhatia et al., 2014; Rincon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: To delay mitotic commitment, Pom1 phosphorylates the C-terminus of Cdr2.
source: To delay mitotic commitment, Pom1 phosphorylates the C-terminus of Cdr2 (Bhatia et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2014), which antagonizes the activating phosphorylation of the Cdr2 kinase domain by the cytosolic CaMKK Ssp1 (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cdr2 localizes at the mid-cell cortex, where it forms large, stable clusters called nodes.
source: Cdr2 localizes at the mid-cell cortex, where it forms large, stable clusters called nodes, which contain many other proteins including a second SAD-family kinase Cdr1 (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Morrell et al., 2004; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Wee1 visits to Cdr2 nodes are only transient.
source: In contrast to the stable Cdr1 and Cdr2 association to the nodes, Wee1 visits are only transient (Allard et al., 2018; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Wee1 visits to Cdr2 nodes increase in frequency and duration as cells grow.
source: These visits increase in frequency and duration as cells grow, consistent with the idea that Wee1 is inactivated in longer cells to permit CDK1 activation and mitotic entry.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Initial work proposed Pom1 gradients as a means to measure cell size, because total fluorescence measurements of Pom1-GFP along cell length revealed higher medial fluorescence in short than long cells.
source: Initial work proposed Pom1 gradients as a means to measure cell size, because total fluorescence measurements of Pom1-GFP along cell length revealed higher medial fluorescence in short than long cells (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The levels of Cdr2 phosphorylation by Ssp1 increase during G2, consistent with a progressive decrease in Pom1-dependent inhibition.
source: First, the levels of Cdr2 phosphorylation by Ssp1 increase during G2, consistent with a progressive decrease in Pom1-dependent inhibition (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Pom1 suppresses Wee1 visits in short cells.
source: Second, the frequency and duration of Wee1 visits to Cdr2 nodes increase as cells grow, with direct evidence showing that Pom1 suppresses Wee1 visits in short cells (Allard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Pom1 re-localization to cell sides leads to strong mitotic delay.
source: In addition, Pom1 re-localization to cell sides, which is prominent upon glucose starvation, leads to strong mitotic delay (Kelkar and Martin, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Subsequent analyses of cortical fluorescence profiles on confocal mid-plane images failed to detect significant differences in the levels of Pom1-GFP at mid-cell between short and long cells.
source: However, subsequent analyses of cortical fluorescence profiles on confocal mid-plane images failed to detect significant differences in the levels of Pom1-GFP at mid-cell between short and long cells, raising questions about the previously proposed model (Bhatia et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: pom1∆ cells retain homeostatic capacity.
source: This also led to the suggestion that Cdr2, not Pom1, may be the critical cell size sensor in the pathway (Pan et al., 2014). Thus, there is currently a controversy between the invariant Pom1 levels at mid-cell and the size-dependent effect of Pom1 on Cdr2 function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The Pom1-mEos3.2 distribution along cortical profiles was indistinguishable from that of Pom1-GFP.
source: The Pom1-mEos3.2 distribution along cortical profiles was indistinguishable from that of Pom1-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The residence time of Pom1 exhibits a multimodal distribution, which could be fitted with a bi-exponential decay corresponding to short and long residence times.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the residence time exhibits a multimodal distribution, which could be fitted with a bi-exponential decay corresponding to short and long residence times, or fast and slow dissociation rates (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: The majority of Pom1 molecules (76%) comprise the fast-dissociating part, while the remaining (23%) dissociate more slowly.
source: The majority of Pom1 molecules (76%) comprise the fast-dissociating part, while the remaining (23%) dissociate more slowly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of residence time data.

claim: Both Pom1WT and Pom1KD showed fast and slow-dissociating populations, with a similar fold difference in dissociation rates between the two populations (2.8x and 2.7x, respectively).
source: Both Pom1WT and Pom1KD showed fast and slow-dissociating populations, with a similar fold difference in dissociation rates between the two populations (2.8x and 2.7x, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of dissociation rate data.

claim: Pom1 activity, which leads to auto-phosphorylation, promotes a faster dissociation rate of Pom1 from the membrane.
source: Thus, Pom1 activity, which leads to auto-phosphorylation, promotes a faster dissociation rate of Pom1 from the membrane, in agreement with previous biochemical observations (Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of Pom1WT and Pom1KD dissociation rates.

claim: The track duration teff and diffusion coefficient Deff were inversely correlated.
source: We found that the track duration teff and diffusion coefficient Deff were inversely correlated (Figure 2A), with shorter tracks exhibiting faster diffusion and longer tracks exhibiting slower diffusion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Slowly diffusing Pom1 molecules present slow dissociation dynamics, and vice versa.
source: Since long residence times imply a slower dissociation time, slowly diffusing Pom1 molecules present slow dissociation dynamics, and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the inverse correlation between track duration and diffusion coefficient.

claim: In larger, slowly diffusing clusters, Pom1 remains more stably associated with the membrane.
source: This suggests that in larger, slowly diffusing clusters, Pom1 remains more stably associated with the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the correlation between diffusion and dissociation.

claim: Individual Pom1 molecules will only travel a maximum distance of 0.8 µm before detaching from the plasma membrane.
source: From these values, we can estimate a maximum travelled distance of 0.8 µm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on calculations from diffusion coefficients and binding times.

claim: It is unlikely that individual Pom1 molecules continuously track from cell pole to cell sides.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that individual molecules continuously track from cell pole to cell sides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the maximum travelled distance calculation.

claim: The distribution of diffusion coefficients of Pom1WT at the cell pole was shifted toward slower values compared to Pom1WT at the cell sides.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of diffusion coefficients was shifted toward slower values compared to Pom1WT at the cell sides (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: At the cell pole, a much smaller proportion of Pom1WT molecules were fast-diffusing compared with the sides, very similar to the proportion observed for Pom1KD.
source: Indeed, when using the same thresholds as above, a much smaller proportion of molecules were fast-diffusing compared with the sides (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), very similar to the proportion observed for Pom1KD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The diffusion behavior of Pom1WT at the cell pole is consistent with Pom1 being mainly in its dephosphorylated state at this location.
source: This is consistent with Pom1 being mainly in its dephosphorylated state at the cell pole, in agreement with the presence of the Tea4-PP1 phosphatase at this location (Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the diffusion data.

claim: Pom1WT exhibits a change in the relative proportion of molecules along the gradient: the proportion of fast diffusive Pom1 remained relatively constant, but the proportion of intermediate and slow diffusive Pom1 decreased.
source: Interestingly, when we considered fast, intermediate and slow populations separately, we found that Pom1WT exhibits a change in the relative proportion of molecules: the proportion of fast diffusive Pom1 remained relatively constant all along the gradient, but the proportion of intermediate and slow diffusive Pom1 decreased, resulting in a relative increase in the fast population (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2G.

claim: The proportions of fast, intermediate and slow diffusive populations of Pom1KD remain balanced all along the gradient.
source: In contrast, the proportions of fast, intermediate and slow diffusive populations of Pom1KD remain balanced all along the gradient, leading to a nearly constant ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of diffusion data.

claim: A Pom1 fragment containing amino acids 305 to 510 can efficiently bind the plasma membrane.
source: Previous work has shown that Pom1 interacts with lipids (Hachet et al., 2011) and a fragment containing amino acids 305 to 510 can efficiently bind the plasma membrane (Figure 3A, fragment #1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: BH-search prediction identified two potential membrane binding sites in the Pom1 305-510 fragment.
source: A BH-search prediction (Brzeska et al., 2010) performed for this fragment identified two potential membrane binding sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: The first membrane binding region (MB1; aa 423–444) is within a 22aa-long sequence that is identical in the four Schizosaccharomyces species.
source: These two regions map to the most conserved sequences in the 305–510 fragment: the first (aa 437–444) is within a 22aa-long sequence (MB1; aa 423–444) that is identical in the four Schizosaccharomyces species (S. pombe, S. octosporus, S. japonicus, and S. cryophilus), the second (aa 480–492) falls within a weak amphipathic helix prediction (MB2; aa 477–494) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 3A.

claim: A minimal 468-510aa fragment containing the putative amphipathic helix was sufficient for membrane binding.
source: Progressive N-terminal truncations showed that a minimal 468-510aa fragment (fragment #5) containing the putative amphipathic helix was sufficient for membrane binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3D.

claim: Converting the hydrophobic Ile494 to the polar, uncharged Asp residue (I494N) disrupted membrane binding in the minimal fragment.
source: In this fragment, converting the hydrophobic Ile494 to the polar, uncharged Asp residue disrupted membrane binding (I494N, fragment #6), indicating that Pom1 binds the membrane through the predicted amphipathic helix.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3D.

claim: The I494N point mutation in the full 305-510aa fragment did not disrupt cortical localization, indicating the presence of a second lipid-binding domain.
source: However, the same point mutation in the full 305-510aa fragment (fragment #7) did not disrupt cortical localization, indicating the presence of a second lipid-binding domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3D.

claim: Combining both the I494N and MB1* mutations within fragment 305–510 yielded a fully cytosolic localization.
source: However, combining both the I494N and MB1* mutations within fragment 305–510 yielded a fully cytosolic localization (fragment #9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3D.

claim: Pom1 localization to the plasma membrane relies on two adjacent lipid-binding motifs.
source: We conclude that Pom1 localization to the plasma membrane relies on two adjacent lipid-binding motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the fragment analysis.

claim: Individual I494N and MB1* mutations in full-length Pom1 led to a decrease of fluorescence intensity at the cell tip.
source: Individual I494N and MB1* mutations led to a decrease of fluorescence intensity at the cell tip, which was exacerbated in the double mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3E.

claim: In the double mutant (MB1* I494N), small Pom1 clusters were visible at the cell tips, likely due to Pom1 direct binding to Tea4 through PxxP motifs.
source: Nevertheless, in this double mutant small Pom1 clusters were visible at the cell tips, likely due to Pom1 direct binding to the phosphatase regulatory subunit Tea4 through PxxP motifs (Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3E.

claim: Additional mutagenesis of the five PxxP motifs in combination with the MB1* and I494N mutations rendered Pom1 entirely cytosolic.
source: Indeed, additional mutagenesis of the five previously identified PxxP motifs in combination with the MB1* and I494N mutations rendered Pom1 entirely cytosolic.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by localization data in Figure 3E.

claim: A decrease in the number of phosphorylation sites led to a gradual flattening of the gradient shape manifested in a decrease of Pom1 intensity at the cell tip and an increase at the cell middle.
source: A decrease in the number of phosphorylation sites led to a gradual flattening of the gradient shape manifested in a decrease of Pom1 intensity at the cell tip and an increase at the cell middle (Figure 4B–C, left panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The gradual change of gradient shape indicates the additive nature of multiple autophosphorylation events.
source: The gradual change of gradient shape indicates the additive nature of multiple autophosphorylation events and reveals that no particular site contributes to Pom1 gradient shape more than another.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the phospho-site mutant data.

claim: The gradient shape of the Pom15A mutant was indistinguishable from those of Pom16A and inactive Pom1KD.
source: The gradient shape of the Pom15A mutant was indistinguishable from those of the previously described non-phosphorylatable Pom16A and inactive Pom1KD (Hachet et al., 2011), indicating that these five sites represent the principal sites modulating Pom1 localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The distribution of diffusion coefficients of Pom13A was intermediate between Pom1WT and Pom1KD.
source: The distribution of diffusion coefficients was also intermediate between Pom1WT and Pom1KD (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: In tea4∆ cells, all Pom1 phospho-mutants bound the cortex nearly uniformly.
source: In tea4Δ cells, all Pom1 phospho-mutants bound the cortex nearly uniformly (Figure 4A, bottom row), with levels that increased with the number of phospho-site mutations (Figure 4B–C, right panels), and a concomitant decrease in Pom1 cytosolic levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Each phosphorylation event progressively lowers membrane affinity to reduce Pom1 binding in the medial region.
source: These data are in agreement with the idea that each phosphorylation event progressively lowers membrane affinity to reduce Pom1 binding in the medial region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the tea4∆ data.

claim: The flatter gradients observed in the Pom1 phospho-mutants are due to both a reduction of Pom1 detachment from the membrane and an increase in Pom1 attachment to the membrane at mid-cell.
source: This suggests that the flatter gradients observed in the Pom1 phospho-mutants are not only due to a reduction of Pom1 detachment from the membrane, allowing lateral diffusion over a longer distance, but also to an increase in Pom1 attachment to the membrane at mid-cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data comparing WT and tea4∆ cells.

claim: Pom1 auto-phosphorylation both favors its detachment from, and prevents its attachment to, the membrane.
source: Thus, Pom1 auto-phosphorylation both favors its detachment from, and prevents its attachment to, the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the phospho-mutant analysis.

claim: Pom11A, Pom12A and Pom13A all showed a loss of negative correlation of decay length to Pom1 concentration at the cell tip.
source: Pom11A, Pom12A and Pom13A all showed a loss of negative correlation of decay length to Pom1 concentration at the cell tip (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: Pom1 phospho-mutants poorly correct intrinsic variations of Pom1 concentrations at the cell tips.
source: Thus, these Pom1 mutants poorly correct intrinsic variations of Pom1 concentrations at the cell tips.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the decay length correlation data.

claim: The decrease in the coefficient of variation at cell tips and cell sides is much smaller for Pom11A, Pom12A and Pom13A compared to Pom1WT.
source: While we confirm this observation with our current data set, the decrease in the coefficient of variation at cell tips and cell sides is much smaller for Pom11A, Pom12A and Pom13A (from 9.6-fold for Pom1WT to 6.6 for Pom11A, 5.8 for Pom12A, and 4.2 for Pom13A; Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: The Pom1 phosphorylation cycle directly contributes to Pom1 gradient shape robustness.
source: We conclude that the Pom1 phosphorylation cycle directly contributes to Pom1 gradient shape robustness.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the coefficient of variation analysis.

claim: A gradual increase in cell length at division was observed in mutants of the phospho-site allelic series.
source: Consistent with previous reports that Pom16A and Pom1 overexpression lead to cell size increase at division (Hachet et al., 2011; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009), we observed a gradual increase in cell length at division in mutants of the phospho-site allelic series (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Cell length at division was strongly correlated with the medial cortical Pom1 levels.
source: Cell length at division was strongly correlated with the medial cortical Pom1 levels (Figure 5B), consistent with the idea that medial Pom1 levels set the cell division size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The progressive increase in cortical Pom1 in Pom1 phospho-mutants correlated with an increase of cell length in tea4Δ background.
source: To evaluate the relative contributions of cytosolic and cortical Pom1 in Cdr2 inhibition, independently of gradient formation, we obtained the same measurements in tea4∆ cells: the progressive increase in cortical Pom1 in Pom1 phospho-mutants also correlated with an increase of cell length in tea4Δ background (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The medial cortical pool of Pom1 is the relevant pool for cell size regulation.
source: We conclude that the medial cortical pool of Pom1 is the relevant pool for cell size regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the correlation analyses.

claim: Pom11A-GFP, Pom13A-GFP and Pom15A-GFP show increased cortical levels compared to Pom1WT-GFP by TIRF imaging.
source: Pom11A-GFP, Pom13A-GFP and Pom15A-GFP show increased cortical levels compared to Pom1WT-GFP (p=0.01, p=10−14, p=10−41, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TIRF imaging data in Figure 5C.

claim: Cytosolic GFP expressed under the pom1 promoter could not be detected by TIRF though it was seen by epifluorescence.
source: First, cytosolic GFP, expressed under the pom1 promoter, could not be detected by TIRF though it was seen by epifluorescence, confirming that the evanescent field detects only cortical molecules (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 5C.

claim: Pom1-GFP in tea4∆ cells revealed a cortical signal by TIRF imaging.
source: By contrast, Pom1-GFP in tea4∆ cells, which by confocal microscopy is not detected at the cortex (see Figure 4A; Hachet et al., 2011; Kokkoris et al., 2014; Padte et al., 2006), revealed a cortical signal by TIRF imaging (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TIRF imaging data in Figure 5C.

claim: In tea4∆, Pom1 formed cortical clusters, though cluster number, size and intensity were lower than in wild type.
source: In tea4∆, Pom1 formed cortical clusters, though cluster number, size and intensity were lower than in wild type (Figure 5D), which likely explains why the cortical Pom1WT signal in tea4Δ is virtually indistinguishable from the cytosolic signal by confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: TIRF provides a highly specific and sensitive imaging setup for Pom1 clusters at the yeast cortex.
source: We conclude that TIRF provides a highly specific and sensitive imaging setup for Pom1 clusters at the yeast cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Cdr2-GFP formed stable nodes at mid-cell, which did not move substantially over 60 s.
source: In TIRF timelapse imaging, Cdr2-GFP formed stable nodes at mid-cell, which did not move substantially over 60 s (Allard et al., 2018), whereas Pom1-GFP clusters were highly dynamic (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TIRF imaging data in Figure 5E.

claim: Pom1-GFP clusters exhibited an array of dynamics with clusters moving laterally, splitting or merging.
source: Fast 100 ms acquisition intervals were used to monitor Pom1 clusters, which exhibited an array of dynamics with clusters moving laterally, splitting or merging.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TIRF imaging data in Figure 5F and Videos 1-2.

claim: Pom1 clusters often recombine and can gain and lose individual Pom1 molecules over time.
source: These fluctuations in the fluorescence signal of individual clusters indicate that clusters often recombine and can gain and loose individual Pom1 molecules over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the cluster dynamics observed by TIRF.

claim: Pom1 cluster lifetimes ranged to over 8 s, the length of the imaging timeframe.
source: To estimate the lifetime of individual clusters, we followed 38 Pom1 clusters in 12 cells. The cluster lifetime from appearance to disappearance or splitting of the cluster ranged to over 8 s, the length of the imaging timeframe (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: Pom1 cluster lifetimes are substantially longer than the binding time obtained by PALM imaging for individual molecules (around 1 to 3 s).
source: They are also substantially longer than the binding time obtained by PALM imaging for individual molecules (around 1 to 3 s, see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing TIRF and PALM measurements.

claim: Individual Pom1 molecules turn over within single clusters.
source: These observations further support the idea that individual Pom1 molecules turn over within single clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the difference in lifetimes.

claim: Pom1 clusters are the functional units shaping the gradient, as their longer residence time would permit diffusion from the cell pole all the way to the zone of action at mid-cell.
source: Therefore, we propose that Pom1 clusters are the functional units shaping the gradient, as their longer residence time would permit diffusion from the cell pole all the way to the zone of action at mid-cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a proposed model based on the cluster lifetime data.

claim: Laterally moving Pom1 clusters randomly collide into Cdr2 nodes.
source: We observed a very similar pattern for Pom1 in the non-node-associated ROIs, which suggests that laterally moving Pom1 clusters randomly collide into Cdr2 nodes (Figure 6C), distinct from the targeted visits from the cytosol reported for Wee1 (Allard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The average Pom1 intensity at all measured Cdr2 nodes was significantly higher in short (6 to 8 µm) than long (12 to 14 µm) cells.
source: Remarkably, when we clustered the data according to cell length, the average Pom1 intensity at all measured Cdr2 nodes was significantly higher in short (6 to 8 µm) than long (12 to 14 µm) cells in three independent experimental repeats (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: In short cells, a higher proportion of Cdr2 clusters were continuously occupied by Pom1 over the 60-s imaging period.
source: We observed a similar pattern in the duration of Pom1-Cdr2 encounters, which we defined as the length of time the Pom1-GFP value at a Cdr2 node remained above a defined fluorescence threshold: In short cells, a higher proportion of Cdr2 clusters were continuously occupied by Pom1 over the 60-s imaging period (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Pom1 levels were higher in the middle of short than long cells as measured by total medial Pom1 TIRF signal.
source: Consistent with the observation that Pom1 behavior is similar at and in the vicinity of Cdr2 nodes, measuring the total medial Pom1 TIRF signal gave similar results: Pom1 levels were higher in the middle of short than long cells (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The medial cortical Pom1 levels decrease as cells grow, consistent with cell length-dependent relief of Pom1 inhibition.
source: Thus, the medial cortical Pom1 levels, which are those critical for Cdr2 regulation, decrease as cells grow, consistent with cell length-dependent relief of Pom1 inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the TIRF imaging data.

claim: The buffering of the Pom1 concentration gradient relies on its multi-phosphorylation reaction.
source: We confirm experimentally that the buffering of the Pom1 concentration gradient relies on its multi-phosphorylation reaction and establish that Pom1 molecules turn over within membrane-bound clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion of the work.

claim: Pom1 gradients formed by diffusion of Pom1 clusters reach the middle of short but not long cells.
source: By specifically imaging the relevant pool of Pom1 at the mid-cell cortex, we now unequivocally show that Pom1 gradients formed by diffusion of Pom1 clusters reach the middle of short but not long cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion of the work.

claim: Clusters act as a diffusion unit, whose regenerating capacity is reduced via progressive auto-phosphorylation with time/distance from the cell pole.
source: Thus, clusters act as a diffusion unit, whose regenerating capacity is reduced via progressive auto-phosphorylation with time/distance from the cell pole.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: Pom1 likely exerts its inhibitory action primarily on short cells, when its medial concentration is highest.
source: Pom1 likely exerts its inhibitory action primarily on short cells, when its medial concentration is highest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Cell growth promotes both a decrease in Pom1 levels and an increase in the number of Cdr2 nodes at mid-cell, enhancing the activation of Cdr2 in long cells.
source: Thus, cell growth, by both promoting a decrease in Pom1 levels and an increase in the number of Cdr2 nodes at mid-cell, enhances the activation of Cdr2 in long cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.
